claim: PP1 relies on association with PP1-interacting proteins (PIPs) to generate substrate-specific PIP/PP1 holoenzymes.
source: Phosphoprotein phosphatase 1 (PP1) relies on association with PP1-interacting proteins (PIPs) to generate substrate-specific PIP/PP1 holoenzymes, but the lack of well-defined substrates has hindered elucidation of the mechanisms involved.
evidence: This is a statement about PP1 function supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: The Phactr1 PIP confers sequence specificity on the Phactr1/PP1 holoenzyme by remodelling the PP1 hydrophobic substrate groove.
source: We previously demonstrated that the Phactr1 PIP confers sequence specificity on the Phactr1/PP1 holoenzyme by remodelling the PP1 hydrophobic substrate groove.
evidence: This claim references previous work by the authors demonstrating this mechanism.

claim: Phactr1 defines a group of 'RVxF-ΦΦ-R-W' PIPs that all interact with PP1 in a similar fashion.
source: Phactr1 defines a group of 'RVxF-ΦΦ-R-W' PIPs that all interact with PP1 in a similar fashion.
evidence: This is based on structural alignment data and previous characterization of these PIPs.

claim: The four Phactr proteins confer identical sequence specificities on their holoenzymes.
source: We show that the four Phactr proteins confer identical sequence specificities on their holoenzymes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the PP1-Phactr fusion protein studies and phosphoproteomics.

claim: 4E-BP and p70 S6K translational regulators are substrates for the Neurabin/Spinophilin PIPs.
source: We identify the 4E-BP and p70 S6K translational regulators as substrates for the Neurabin/Spinophilin PIPs, implicated in neuronal plasticity, pointing to a role for their holoenzymes in mTORC1-dependent translational control.
evidence: This is supported by phosphoproteomics data and biochemical validation experiments.

claim: Substrate recruitment and catalytic efficiency of the PP1-Neurabin and PP1-Spinophilin fusions is primarily determined by substrate interaction with the PDZ domain adjoining their RVxF-ΦΦ-R-W motifs.
source: Biochemical and structural experiments show that in contrast to the Phactrs, substrate recruitment and catalytic efficiency of the PP1-Neurabin and PP1-Spinophilin fusions is primarily determined by substrate interaction with the PDZ domain adjoining their RVxF-ΦΦ-R-W motifs, rather than by recognition of the remodelled PP1 hydrophobic groove.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assays with synthetic peptides and structural analysis.

claim: PIPs that interact with PP1 in a similar manner use different mechanisms to ensure substrate selectivity.
source: Thus, even PIPs that interact with PP1 in a similar manner use different mechanisms to ensure substrate selectivity.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of Phactr and Neurabin/Spinophilin substrate recognition mechanisms.

claim: PP1 is a member of the PPP superfamily of protein phosphatases.
source: Phosphoprotein phosphatase 1 (PP1) is a member of the PPP superfamily of protein phosphatases, responsible for most cellular serine/threonine dephosphorylation (Bollen et al., 2010; Brautigan and Shenolikar, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: PP1 is responsible for most cellular serine/threonine dephosphorylation.
source: Phosphoprotein phosphatase 1 (PP1) is a member of the PPP superfamily of protein phosphatases, responsible for most cellular serine/threonine dephosphorylation (Bollen et al., 2010; Brautigan and Shenolikar, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The three PP1 isoforms possess a central metal-binding active centre from which radiate three putative substrate-binding grooves.
source: The three PP1 isoforms possess a central metal-binding active centre from which radiate three putative substrate-binding grooves (Egloff et al., 1995; Goldberg et al., 1995), but have little intrinsic sequence specificity (Hoermann et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on structural studies cited in the text.

claim: PP1 has little intrinsic sequence specificity.
source: The three PP1 isoforms possess a central metal-binding active centre from which radiate three putative substrate-binding grooves (Egloff et al., 1995; Goldberg et al., 1995), but have little intrinsic sequence specificity (Hoermann et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: PP1 substrate specificity and activity are controlled by over 200 PP1-interacting proteins (PIPs).
source: Instead, PP1 substrate specificity and activity are controlled by over 200 PP1-interacting proteins (PIPs), which use a number of short linear motifs (SLiMs) to dock with distinct regions of the PP1 surface, including the substrate-binding grooves (Cohen, 2002; Bollen et al., 2010; Casamayor and Ariño, 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: PIPs use short linear motifs (SLiMs) to dock with distinct regions of the PP1 surface.
source: Instead, PP1 substrate specificity and activity are controlled by over 200 PP1-interacting proteins (PIPs), which use a number of short linear motifs (SLiMs) to dock with distinct regions of the PP1 surface, including the substrate-binding grooves (Cohen, 2002; Bollen et al., 2010; Casamayor and Ariño, 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The Phactr family of actin-regulated PP1 cofactors are the only PIPs known to directly impose substrate sequence specificity at the dephosphorylation site itself.
source: The Phactr family of actin-regulated PP1 cofactors are the only PIPs known to directly impose substrate sequence specificity at the dephosphorylation site itself (Fedoryshchak et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors.

claim: The Phactrs belong to a small subset of RVxF-ΦΦ-R PIPs that make an additional PP1 contact through a 'W' SLIM.
source: Structural alignment showed that the Phactrs belong to a small subset of RVxF-ΦΦ-R PIPs whose shared trajectory across the PP1 surface continues to the edge of the hydrophobic groove, making an additional PP1 contact through an additional motif that we termed the 'W' SLIM (Ragusa et al., 2010; Choy et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2015; Fedoryshchak et al., 2020; Yan et al., 2021; Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on structural alignment data and previous studies, with reference to figures.

claim: RVxF-ΦΦ-R-W string PIPs include Neurabin/Spinophilin (PPP1R9A/B).
source: These 'RVxF-ΦΦ-R-W string' PIPs include Neurabin/Spinophilin (PPP1R9A/B), which play important roles in PP1-dependent regulation of neuronal plasticity (Allen et al., 1997; Burnett et al., 1998, reviewed by Sarrouilhe et al., 2006; Foley et al., 2021)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Neurabin/Spinophilin play important roles in PP1-dependent regulation of neuronal plasticity.
source: These 'RVxF-ΦΦ-R-W string' PIPs include Neurabin/Spinophilin (PPP1R9A/B), which play important roles in PP1-dependent regulation of neuronal plasticity (Allen et al., 1997; Burnett et al., 1998, reviewed by Sarrouilhe et al., 2006; Foley et al., 2021)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: RVxF-ΦΦ-R-W string PIPs include PNUTS (PPP1R10).
source: PNUTS (PPP1R10), which regulates PolII and chromatin dynamics (Lee et al., 2010; Cortazar et al., 2019)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PNUTS regulates PolII and chromatin dynamics.
source: PNUTS (PPP1R10), which regulates PolII and chromatin dynamics (Lee et al., 2010; Cortazar et al., 2019)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: RVxF-ΦΦ-R-W string PIPs include PPP1R15A/B.
source: and PPP1R15A/B, which mediate translational regulation through control of eIF2α dephosphorylation (Novoa et al., 2001; Chen et al., 2015; Yan et al., 2021; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and reference to a figure.

claim: PPP1R15A/B mediate translational regulation through control of eIF2α dephosphorylation.
source: and PPP1R15A/B, which mediate translational regulation through control of eIF2α dephosphorylation (Novoa et al., 2001; Chen et al., 2015; Yan et al., 2021; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In the Phactr1-PP1 holoenzyme, Phactr1 sequences C-terminal to the RVxF-ΦΦ-R-W string interact with the PP1 hydrophobic groove to form a composite hydrophobic pocket.
source: In the Phactr1-PP1 holoenzyme, Phactr1 sequences C-terminal to the RVxF-ΦΦ-R-W string interact with the PP1 hydrophobic groove to form a composite hydrophobic pocket, topped by a basic rim.
evidence: This is based on previous structural and biochemical studies by the authors.

claim: The Phactr1-PP1 holoenzyme imposes strong sequence selectivity on substrates, favouring hydrophobic residues at positions +4/+5 relative to the phosphorylated residue, within an acidic context (consensus pS/T-x(2-3)-Φ-L, the 'LLD motif').
source: This imposes strong sequence selectivity on substrates, favouring hydrophobic residues at positions +4/+5 relative to the phosphorylated residue, within an acidic context (consensus pS/T-x(2-3)-Φ-L, the 'LLD motif').
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors characterizing substrate specificity.

claim: A PP1-Phactr1 fusion protein comprising PP1(1–304) linked to Phactr1 sequences from residue 526 maintains the specificity of the Phactr1-PP1 holoenzyme.
source: Strikingly, this specificity is maintained in a PP1-Phactr1 fusion protein comprising PP1(1–304) linked to Phactr1 sequences from residue 526, just C-terminal to its RVxF motif (Fedoryshchak et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors.

claim: Neurabin and Spinophilin remodel the PP1 hydrophobic groove differently from Phactr1.
source: Neurabin and Spinophilin remodel the PP1 hydrophobic groove differently from Phactr1, generating a structurally distinct surface on the holoenzyme, and it is likely that the other RVxF-ΦΦ-R-W PIPs do so as well (Ragusa et al., 2010; Fedoryshchak et al., 2020) (see Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on structural studies cited in the text and shown in figures.

claim: Neurabin and Spinophilin contain a PDZ domain previously suggested to be involved in substrate recruitment.
source: We use the PP1-PIP fusion approach to show that the four Phactr1 holoenzymes have indistinguishable substrate specificities and to identify novel candidate substrates for the other RVxF-ΦΦ-R-W PIP/PP1 complexes. We use 4E-BP1, a new Neurabin/PP1 substrate, to show that unlike the Phactr1/PP1 holoenzyme, substrate specificity of Neurabin/PP1 is largely determined by interaction with the Neurabin PDZ domain rather than the primary sequences of the dephosphorylation site itself.
evidence: This is based on previous suggestions in the literature and confirmed by the current study.

claim: PP1-Phactr1 expression was induced by tetracycline.
source: PP1-Phactr1 expression was induced by tetracycline as indicated.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Tetracycline induction of PP1-Phactr1 leads to dephosphorylation of IRSp53 S455 and Afadin S1275.
source: Phosphorylation of Phactr1/PP1 substrates IRSp53 S455 and Afadin S1275 is shown below.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B with immunoblotting data.

claim: Afadin pS1275 was dephosphorylated by all four PP1-Phactr fusions.
source: Afadin pS1275 was dephosphorylated by all four PP1-Phactr fusions, but not by the other PP1-PIP fusions (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C with immunoblotting data.

claim: Afadin pS1275 was not dephosphorylated by PP1-Neurabin, PP1-Spinophilin, PP1-R15A, PP1-R15B, or PP1-PNUTS fusions.
source: Afadin pS1275 was dephosphorylated by all four PP1-Phactr fusions, but not by the other PP1-PIP fusions (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C with immunoblotting data.

claim: Alanine substitution of IRSp53 L460 impairs dephosphorylation by all the PP1-Phactr fusions.
source: In this setting, alanine substitution of IRSp53 L460, which contacts the novel Phactr1/PP1 hydrophobic pocket and impairs dephosphorylation by the intact Phactr1/PP1 holoenzyme (Fedoryshchak et al., 2020), also impaired dephosphorylation by all the PP1-Phactr fusions, indicating that they recognise phosphorylated IRSp53 in a similar way (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B with immunoblotting data.

claim: The IRSp53 L460A peptide is significantly less reactive than the IRSp53WT peptide for each of the four PP1-Phactr fusions (p<0.05 for each fusion).
source: For each of the four PP1-Phactr fusions, the IRSp53 L460A peptide is significantly less reactive than the IRSp53WT peptide (p<0.05 for each fusion).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B with statistical analysis.

claim: PP1 exhibited little sequence specificity, other than a preference for positively charged residues in positions −3, –1, and +3 to the dephosphorylation site.
source: In agreement with previous results (Hoermann et al., 2020), PP1 exhibited little sequence specificity, other than a preference for positively charged residues in positions −3, –1, and +3 to the dephosphorylation site (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is based on phosphoproteomics data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B, consistent with previous studies.

claim: Expression of PP1-Phactr1 revealed numerous phosphorylation sites that were specifically depleted compared with cells expressing PP1α alone.
source: Expression of PP1-Phactr1 revealed numerous phosphorylation sites that were specifically depleted compared with cells expressing PP1α alone (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C with phosphoproteomics data.

claim: The population of phosphorylation sites depleted by PP1-Phactr1 contained many of the Phactr1/PP1 holoenzyme substrates previously identified in neurons or NIH3T3 fibroblasts, including IRSp53 pS455 and Afadin pS1275.
source: This population contained many of the Phactr1/PP1 holoenzyme substrates previously identified in neurons or NIH3T3 fibroblasts, including IRSp53 pS455 and Afadin pS1275 (Figure 2C; Fedoryshchak et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on comparison with previous studies and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Of the 28 top Phactr1/PP1 hits previously identified in NIH3T3 cells, 18 were detectable in the 293 system, of which 13 also registered as PP1-Phactr1 hits.
source: Of the 28 top Phactr1/PP1 hits previously identified in NIH3T3 cells, 18 were detectable in the 293 system, of which 13 also registered as PP1-Phactr1 hits (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C comparing data from different cell systems.

claim: The putative PP1-Phactr1 substrates were substantially enriched in the Phactr1/PP1 consensus dephosphorylation motif S/T-x2,3-Φ-L.
source: The putative PP1-Phactr1 substrates were also substantially enriched in the Phactr1/PP1 consensus dephosphorylation motif S/T-x2,3-Φ-L (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D with enrichment analysis.

claim: The profiles of PP1-Phactr2, PP1-Phactr3, and PP1-Phactr4 cells were substantially similar to that of PP1-Phactr1.
source: The profiles of PP1-Phactr2, PP1-Phactr3, and PP1-Phactr4 cells were substantially similar to that of PP1-Phactr1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–F), exhibiting good overall correlations both between total phosphorylation site profiles (Figure 2B), and significant enrichment for both the S/T-x2,3-Φ-L motif and specific Phactr1/PP1 substrates (Figure 2D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is shown in multiple figures with phosphoproteomics data and correlation analysis.

claim: Over 60% of the depleted phosphorylation sites were in common between all four PP1-Phactr fusions.
source: over 60% of the depleted phosphorylation sites were in common between all four fusions (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E with a Venn diagram.

claim: The PP1-Phactr fusions recapitulate the specificity of the Phactr1/PP1 holoenzyme.
source: These data show that the PP1-Phactr fusions recapitulate the specificity of the Phactr1/PP1 holoenzyme.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of fusion protein data with previous holoenzyme data.

claim: PPP1R15A has a well-validated substrate, eIF2α pS51.
source: PPP1R15A has a well-validated substrate, eIF2α pS51 (Novoa et al., 2001), whose effective dephosphorylation requires additional recruitment of G-actin to the PPP1R15A/PP1 complex (Chen et al., 2015; Yan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Effective dephosphorylation of eIF2α pS51 by PPP1R15A/PP1 requires additional recruitment of G-actin to the complex.
source: PPP1R15A has a well-validated substrate, eIF2α pS51 (Novoa et al., 2001), whose effective dephosphorylation requires additional recruitment of G-actin to the PPP1R15A/PP1 complex (Chen et al., 2015; Yan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The eIF2α pS51 phosphorylation site was not detected in the dataset.
source: The eIF2α pS51 phosphorylation site was not detected in the dataset, however, and no other phosphorylation sites were detectably depleted, apart from PPP6R1 S531, in cells expressing PPP1R15B (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is a negative result from the phosphoproteomics experiment.

claim: Expression of the PP1-PNUTS fusion led to specific depletion of phosphorylation sites from CXXC1/CFP1 and SET1B.
source: Expression of the PP1-PNUTS fusion, which includes sequences that recruit WDR82 (Lee et al., 2010), led to specific depletion of phosphorylation sites from CXXC1/CFP1 and SET1B, which along with WDR82 are components of the COMPASS histone lysine N-methyl transferase complexes (Cenik and Shilatifard, 2021; Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C with phosphoproteomics data.

claim: CXXC1/CFP1 and SET1B, along with WDR82, are components of the COMPASS histone lysine N-methyl transferase complexes.
source: Expression of the PP1-PNUTS fusion, which includes sequences that recruit WDR82 (Lee et al., 2010), led to specific depletion of phosphorylation sites from CXXC1/CFP1 and SET1B, which along with WDR82 are components of the COMPASS histone lysine N-methyl transferase complexes (Cenik and Shilatifard, 2021; Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: CXXC1/CFP1 and SET1B bear no obvious sequence similarity in the vicinity of the dephosphorylation site.
source: These proteins bear no obvious sequence similarity in the vicinity of the dephosphorylation site (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Neurabin and Spinophilin are two PIPs implicated in neuronal plasticity.
source: Having validated the PP1-PIP fusion approach, we focussed on Neurabin and Spinophilin, two PIPs implicated in neuronal plasticity (Sarrouilhe et al., 2006; Foley et al., 2021), which contain a PDZ domain implicated in recruitment of potential substrates (Burnett et al., 1998; Yan et al., 1999; Sarrouilhe et al., 2006; Kelker et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The Neurabin and Spinophilin PDZ domain is separated from the RVxF-ΦΦ-R-W string by a 5-turn α-helix.
source: The PDZ domain is separated from the RVxF-ΦΦ-R-W string by a 5-turn α-helix, which remodels the PP1 hydrophobic groove in a manner distinct from Phactr1 (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 2G; Ragusa et al., 2010; Fedoryshchak et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on structural data shown in figures and cited studies.

claim: Expression of the PP1-Neurabin or PP1-Spinophilin fusions led to specific depletion of closely related sets of phosphorylation sites.
source: Expression of the PP1-Neurabin or PP1-Spinophilin fusions led to specific depletion of closely related sets of phosphorylation sites (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A and B with phosphoproteomics data.

claim: The phosphorylation sites depleted by PP1-Neurabin or PP1-Spinophilin included multiple sites from the translational inhibitor proteins 4E-BP1 and 4E-BP2.
source: These included multiple sites from the translational inhibitor proteins 4E-BP1 and 4E-BP2.
evidence: This is based on phosphoproteomics data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Levels of total 4E-BP1 and 4E-BP2 proteins were not affected by PP1-Neurabin or PP1-Spinophilin expression.
source: Levels of total 4E-BP1 and 4E-BP2 proteins were not affected (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A with proteomics data.

claim: Phosphorylation sites from DTL and CAMSAP3 were significantly depleted upon expression of both PP1-Spinophilin and PP1-Neurabin fusions.
source: Phosphorylation sites from two other proteins, DTL and CAMSAP3, were also significantly depleted upon expression of both PP1-Spinophilin and PP1-Neurabin fusions, while a further 7 were specific to one fusion or the other (see Discussion).
evidence: This is based on phosphoproteomics data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Apart from a preference for proline at position +1, the sequences of PP1-Neurabin/Spinophilin substrates did not reveal any obvious sequence similarities in the vicinity of the dephosphorylation site.
source: However, apart from a preference for proline at position +1, inspection of these sequences did not reveal any obvious sequence similarities in the vicinity of the dephosphorylation site (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Substrates identified in the PP1-Phactr and PP1-PNUTS screens showed no detectable depletion in PP1-Neurabin/Spinophilin samples, and vice versa.
source: Substrates identified in the PP1-Phactr and PP1-PNUTS screens showed no detectable depletion, and vice versa, indicating that the substrates identified were specific for each fusion.
evidence: This is based on comparison of phosphoproteomics data across different fusion proteins.

claim: Induction of PP1-Neurabin resulted in decreased phosphorylation of 4E-BP1 T70, S65/S101, and possibly T37/T46.
source: Consistent with the phosphoproteomics data, immunoblotting analysis with phosphorylation-specific antibodies demonstrated that induction of PP1-Neurabin resulted in decreased phosphorylation of T70, S65/S101, and possibly T37/T46, while total 4E-BP1 resolved from a heterogeneous distribution to a largely monodisperse species (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D with immunoblotting data.

claim: Induction of PP1-Neurabin caused total 4E-BP1 to resolve from a heterogeneous distribution to a largely monodisperse species.
source: Consistent with the phosphoproteomics data, immunoblotting analysis with phosphorylation-specific antibodies demonstrated that induction of PP1-Neurabin resulted in decreased phosphorylation of T70, S65/S101, and possibly T37/T46, while total 4E-BP1 resolved from a heterogeneous distribution to a largely monodisperse species (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D with immunoblotting data.

claim: The 4E-BPs are critical components of the mTORC1 growth control pathway which couples translation to nutrient availability and extracellular signals.
source: The 4E-BPs are critical components of the mTORC1 growth control pathway which couples translation to nutrient availability and extracellular signals (reviewed by Hoeffer and Klann, 2010; Liu and Sabatini, 2020) (see Discussion).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Phosphorylation of 4E-BPs potentiates translation by inhibiting their ability to sequester EIF4E.
source: Phosphorylation of 4E-BPs potentiates translation by inhibiting their ability to sequester EIF4E (reviewed by Martineau et al., 2013; Romagnoli et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Expression of PP1-Neurabin, but not PP1 alone, suppressed translation in 293 cells.
source: Accordingly, expression of PP1-Neurabin, but not PP1 alone, suppressed translation in 293 cells (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E with a protein synthesis assay.

claim: The Neurabin/PP1 and Spinophilin/PP1 holoenzymes are potential negative regulators of the mTORC1 pathway.
source: These data establish the Neurabin/PP1 and Spinophilin/PP1 holoenzymes as potential negative regulators of the mTORC1 pathway (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D; see Discussion).
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing 4E-BP dephosphorylation and translation suppression.

claim: PP1-Neurabin dephosphorylates 4E-BP1 pT37/46, pS65/101, and pT70 in vitro.
source: Analysis with the phospho-specific antibodies confirmed that pT37/46, pS65/101, and pT70 are all direct targets for dephosphorylation by PP1-Neurabin, with pT70 being somewhat preferred (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A and B with in vitro dephosphorylation assays.

claim: PP1-Neurabin shows a preference for dephosphorylating 4E-BP1 pT70 over other sites.
source: Analysis with the phospho-specific antibodies confirmed that pT37/46, pS65/101, and pT70 are all direct targets for dephosphorylation by PP1-Neurabin, with pT70 being somewhat preferred (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A and B with in vitro dephosphorylation assays.

claim: The 4E-BP C-terminal sequences are similar to those of p70 S6K.
source: The 4E-BP C-terminal sequences are similar to those of p70 S6K, which was previously shown to interact with the Neurabin PDZ domain through a C-terminal PDZ-binding motif (PBM) (Burnett et al., 1998; Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison and previous studies.

claim: p70 S6K was previously shown to interact with the Neurabin PDZ domain through a C-terminal PDZ-binding motif (PBM).
source: The 4E-BP C-terminal sequences are similar to those of p70 S6K, which was previously shown to interact with the Neurabin PDZ domain through a C-terminal PDZ-binding motif (PBM) (Burnett et al., 1998; Figure 4C).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Simple deletion of the 4E-BP1 C-terminal residues substantially blocked phosphorylation of transfected mCherry-4E-BP1.
source: Simple deletion of the 4E-BP1 C-terminal residues substantially blocked phosphorylation of transfected mCherry-4E-BP1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), reflecting the loss of the C-terminal TOR signalling (TOS) motif required for mTORC1 kinase recruitment and 4E-BP1 phosphorylation (Schalm and Blenis, 2002; Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A with immunoblotting data.

claim: The C-terminal TOS motif is required for mTORC1 kinase recruitment and 4E-BP1 phosphorylation.
source: Simple deletion of the 4E-BP1 C-terminal residues substantially blocked phosphorylation of transfected mCherry-4E-BP1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), reflecting the loss of the C-terminal TOR signalling (TOS) motif required for mTORC1 kinase recruitment and 4E-BP1 phosphorylation (Schalm and Blenis, 2002; Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The TOS motif does not include the C-terminal carboxylate, an essential part of the classical PBM.
source: Noting that the TOS motif does not include the C-terminal carboxylate, an essential part of the classical PBM (Harris and Lim, 2001; Tonikian et al., 2008; Subbaiah et al., 2011), we generated mCherry-4E-BP1(118+A): this contains an additional C-terminal alanine, which leaves the TOS motif intact but inactivates the PBM.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about PBM structure supported by citations.

claim: mCherry-4E-BP1(118+A) was efficiently phosphorylated upon expression in 293 cells.
source: Indeed, although mCherry-4E-BP1(118+A) was efficiently phosphorylated upon expression in 293 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), its dephosphorylation in vitro required PP1-Neurabin concentrations some 20–50 times greater than the wildtype protein (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A with immunoblotting data.

claim: Dephosphorylation of mCherry-4E-BP1(118+A) in vitro required PP1-Neurabin concentrations some 20–50 times greater than the wildtype protein.
source: Indeed, although mCherry-4E-BP1(118+A) was efficiently phosphorylated upon expression in 293 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), its dephosphorylation in vitro required PP1-Neurabin concentrations some 20–50 times greater than the wildtype protein (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A and B with in vitro dephosphorylation assays.

claim: The 4E-BP1 C-terminal sequences constitute a PBM.
source: These results suggest that the 4E-BP1 C-terminal sequences constitute a PBM and point to a role for the Neurabin and Spinophilin PDZ domains in substrate recognition.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis and dephosphorylation data.

claim: The 4E-BP1 PBM is identical amongst all three 4E-BP isoforms.
source: The 4E-BP1 PBM, which is identical amongst all three 4E-BP isoforms, bound the PDZ domains with comparable affinities in the micromolar range, and binding was abolished by substitution of the C-terminal hydrophobic residues (Figure 4C and D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison and fluorescence polarization assay data.

claim: The 4E-BP1 PBM bound the Neurabin and Spinophilin PDZ domains with comparable affinities in the micromolar range.
source: The 4E-BP1 PBM, which is identical amongst all three 4E-BP isoforms, bound the PDZ domains with comparable affinities in the micromolar range, and binding was abolished by substitution of the C-terminal hydrophobic residues (Figure 4C and D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C and D with fluorescence polarization assay data.

claim: Binding of the 4E-BP1 PBM to the PDZ domains was abolished by substitution of the C-terminal hydrophobic residues.
source: The 4E-BP1 PBM, which is identical amongst all three 4E-BP isoforms, bound the PDZ domains with comparable affinities in the micromolar range, and binding was abolished by substitution of the C-terminal hydrophobic residues (Figure 4C and D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C and D with fluorescence polarization assay data.

claim: The binding affinities of the 4E-BP1 PBM for the PDZ domains were 10- to 30-fold greater than those of p70 S6K and the RhoGEF Kalirin-7.
source: These binding affinities were 10- to 30-fold greater than those of p70 S6K and the RhoGEF Kalirin-7, which were of order 100 µM, and >100-fold greater than various glutamate receptor C-terminal peptides (Figure 4C and D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C and D with fluorescence polarization assay data.

claim: p70 S6K also functions in the mTORC1 pathway.
source: p70 S6K also functions in the mTORC1 pathway (for reviews, see Liu and Sabatini, 2020; Artemenko et al., 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PP1-Neurabin expression decreased the levels of the p70 S6K activating T389 phosphorylation.
source: Although most of its phosphorylation sites were not detected by phosphoproteomics, immunoblotting experiments demonstrated that PP1-Neurabin expression decreased the levels of the activating T389 phosphorylation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C with immunoblotting data.

claim: PP1-Neurabin dephosphorylated 4E-BP1PBM with a catalytic efficiency some 100-fold greater than PP1 alone.
source: PP1-Neurabin dephosphorylated 4E-BP1PBM with a catalytic efficiency some 100-fold greater than PP1 alone, while peptide 4E-BP1MUT, which cannot bind the Neurabin PDZ domain, was 30-fold less reactive (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A with phosphatase activity assay data.

claim: Peptide 4E-BP1MUT, which cannot bind the Neurabin PDZ domain, was 30-fold less reactive with PP1-Neurabin than 4E-BP1PBM.
source: PP1-Neurabin dephosphorylated 4E-BP1PBM with a catalytic efficiency some 100-fold greater than PP1 alone, while peptide 4E-BP1MUT, which cannot bind the Neurabin PDZ domain, was 30-fold less reactive (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A with phosphatase activity assay data.

claim: PP1-Phactr1 dephosphorylated 4E-BP1PBM and 4E-BP1MUT at rates similar to those achieved by PP1 alone.
source: In contrast, PP1-Phactr1 dephosphorylated 4E-BP1PBM and 4E-BP1MUT at rates similar to those achieved by PP1 alone (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A with phosphatase activity assay data.

claim: The Neurabin sequences, specifically the PDZ domain, play a critical role in specific 4E-BP1 pT70 substrate recognition.
source: The Neurabin sequences, specifically the PDZ domain, thus play a critical role in specific 4E-BP1 pT70 substrate recognition.
evidence: This is inferred from the peptide dephosphorylation assay data.

claim: PP1-Neurabin dephosphorylated IRSp53PBM with somewhat higher catalytic efficiency than 4E-BP1PBM.
source: PP1-Neurabin also dephosphorylated IRSp53PBM, which contains the 4E-BP1 PBM, with somewhat higher catalytic efficiency to that seen with 4E-BP1PBM itself (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B with phosphatase activity assay data.

claim: Dephosphorylation of IRSp53PBM by PP1-Neurabin was entirely dependent on PDZ domain interaction.
source: This was entirely dependent on PDZ domain interaction, IRSp53MUT being ~100-fold less reactive (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B with phosphatase activity assay data.

claim: PP1-Phactr1 dephosphorylated both IRSp53PBM and IRSp53MUT peptides with a similar catalytic efficiency, some 100-fold greater than that seen with PP1 alone.
source: In contrast, PP1-Phactr1 dephosphorylated both IRSp53PBM and IRSp53MUT peptides with a similar catalytic efficiency, some 100-fold greater than that seen with PP1 alone (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B with phosphatase activity assay data.

claim: The PDZ domain plays a critical role in PP1-Neurabin substrate specificity.
source: These results demonstrate the critical role played by the PDZ domain substrate specificity and underscore the role played by PIPs in potentiating the catalytic efficiency of PIP/PP1 complexes.
evidence: This is inferred from the peptide dephosphorylation assay data.

claim: PIPs play a role in potentiating the catalytic efficiency of PIP/PP1 complexes.
source: These results demonstrate the critical role played by the PDZ domain substrate specificity and underscore the role played by PIPs in potentiating the catalytic efficiency of PIP/PP1 complexes.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of PP1 alone versus PP1-PIP fusion activities.

claim: Positions +3 to +6 relative to the dephosphorylation site are critical for recognition of the remodelled hydrophobic groove by Phactr1/PP1.
source: Positions +3 to +6 relative to the dephosphorylation site are critical for recognition of the remodelled hydrophobic groove by Phactr1/PP1 (Fedoryshchak et al., 2020), so we assessed the effect of mutations at these positions on catalytic activity.
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors.

claim: PP1-Neurabin dephosphorylated 4E-BP1PBM containing alanine substitutions at positions +3/4 or +5/6 with slightly increased catalytic efficiency.
source: PP1-Neurabin dephosphorylated 4E-BP1PBM containing alanine substitutions, or IRSp53 sequences, at positions +3/4 or +5/6 with slightly increased catalytic efficiency (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and C with phosphatase activity assay data.

claim: Alanine substitutions at positions +3/4 or +5/6 in 4E-BP1PBM had little effect on dephosphorylation by PP1-Phactr1.
source: These mutations had strikingly different effects on 4E-BP1PBM dephosphorylation by PP1-Phactr1, however. While the alanine substitutions at positions +3/4 or +5/6 had little effect, conversion of +4 to +6 to the IRSp53 sequence LLD increased catalytic efficiency some 20-fold (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and C with phosphatase activity assay data.

claim: Conversion of 4E-BP1PBM positions +4 to +6 to the IRSp53 sequence LLD increased catalytic efficiency by PP1-Phactr1 some 20-fold.
source: These mutations had strikingly different effects on 4E-BP1PBM dephosphorylation by PP1-Phactr1, however. While the alanine substitutions at positions +3/4 or +5/6 had little effect, conversion of +4 to +6 to the IRSp53 sequence LLD increased catalytic efficiency some 20-fold (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and C with phosphatase activity assay data.

claim: Alanine substitution in the groove-interacting region of IRSp53 peptides had no effect on catalytic efficiency with PP1-Neurabin.
source: Similar results were seen with the IRSp53 substrate peptides: alanine substitution in the groove-interacting region had no effect on catalytic efficiency with PP1-Neurabin, but significantly impaired it with PP1-Phactr1 (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and D with phosphatase activity assay data.

claim: Alanine substitution in the groove-interacting region of IRSp53 peptides significantly impaired catalytic efficiency with PP1-Phactr1.
source: Similar results were seen with the IRSp53 substrate peptides: alanine substitution in the groove-interacting region had no effect on catalytic efficiency with PP1-Neurabin, but significantly impaired it with PP1-Phactr1 (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and D with phosphatase activity assay data.

claim: Alanine substitutions at +1 and +2 in 4E-BP1PBM significantly increased catalytic efficiency by both PP1-Neurabin and PP1-Phactr1.
source: Strikingly, alanine substitutions at +1 and+2 in 4E-BP1PBM significantly increased catalytic efficiency by both PP1-Neurabin and PP1-Phactr1, perhaps reflecting changes at the catalytic site itself (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and E; see Discussion).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and E with phosphatase activity assay data.

claim: PP1-Neurabin substrate specificity is driven predominantly by the ability of substrates to interact with the Neurabin PDZ domain rather than the remodelled PP1 hydrophobic groove.
source: Taken together with the results in the preceding section, these data support a model in which PP1-Neurabin substrate specificity is driven predominantly by the ability of substrates to interact with the Neurabin PDZ domain rather than the remodelled PP1 hydrophobic groove (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the peptide dephosphorylation assay data and mutagenesis studies.

claim: The specificity of PP1-Phactr1 is critically dependent on interaction with the remodelled PP1 hydrophobic groove.
source: In contrast, the specificity of PP1-Phactr1, like that of the PP1/Phactr1 holoenzyme, is critically dependent on interaction with the remodelled PP1 hydrophobic groove (Fedoryshchak et al., 2020; Figure 5—figure supplement 2; see Discussion).
evidence: This is based on previous work and the current peptide dephosphorylation data.

claim: The crystal structure of the PP1-4E-BP1/Neurabin complex was determined at 2.36 Å resolution.
source: Accordingly, we constructed an analogous PP1-4E-BP1 substrate fusion, comprising PP1(7–304)/(SG)5/4E-BP1(65–83)/G/4E-BP1(112–118) (Figure 6A), co-expressed it with Neurabin residues 423–593, and determined the crystal structure of the purified complex at 2.36 Å resolution (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1; Table 1; Ragusa et al., 2010).
evidence: This is structural data obtained from X-ray crystallography.

claim: In the PP1-4E-BP1/Neurabin complex, the PP1 catalytic core and Neurabin PDZ sequences were well resolved, along with the 4E-BP1 PBM.
source: In the complex, the PP1 catalytic core and Neurabin PDZ sequences were well resolved, along with the 4E-BP1 PBM, which was docked with the Neurabin PDZ domain (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is structural data from the crystal structure.

claim: The individual domains in the PP1-4E-BP1/Neurabin complex were largely identical to those determined previously for unliganded Neurabin/PP1.
source: The individual domains were largely identical to those determined previously for unliganded Neurabin/PP1 (Ragusa et al., 2010) (PP1(1–304), RMSD 0.22 Å over 269 Cα, PDZ(501–592) RMSD 0.39 Å over 65 Cα).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison with a previously published structure.

claim: The PDZ domain in the Neurabin/PP1-4E-BP1 substrate complex structure is oriented at 22° to that in the unliganded Neurabin/PP1 complex.
source: However, the PDZ domain in our Neurabin/PP1-4E-BP1 substrate complex structure is oriented at 22° to that in the unliganded Neurabin/PP1 complex, reflecting a slight bend in the C-terminal section of the 5-turn α-helix that connects it to the RVxF-ΦΦ-R-W string (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The 4E-BP1 PBM uses a beta-strand addition mechanism to make extensive contacts with the Neurabin PDZ domain.
source: The 4E-BP1 PBM, 113(QFEMDI)118, uses a beta-strand addition mechanism to make extensive contacts with the Neurabin PDZ domain, similar to those seen in other PDZ-ligand complexes, that widen the PBM-binding groove (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is structural data from the crystal structure shown in Figure 6D.

claim: 4E-BP1 F114, M116, and I118 side chains make hydrophobic contacts with the Neurabin PDZ domain.
source: 4E-BP1 F114, M116, and I118 side chains make hydrophobic contacts, while their main chain carbonyl and amide groups, and the C-terminal carboxylate, form an extensive hydrogen bonding network with Neurabin main chain residues L514, G515, I516, I518, and G520 (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is structural data from the crystal structure shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Apart from the C-terminal PBM, the 4E-BP1 T70 substrate sequences were largely unresolved in the crystal structure.
source: Apart from the C-terminal PBM, the 4E-BP1 T70 substrate sequences were largely unresolved in the crystal structure.
evidence: This is a description of the crystal structure data.

claim: No interactions were seen between 4E-BP1 substrate sequences and the remodelled PP1-Neurabin hydrophobic groove in the crystal structure.
source: Unlike the Phactr1 substrate chimera, no interactions were seen with the remodelled PP1-Neurabin hydrophobic groove; and no virtual enzyme-product complex and solvent phosphate were detected at the active site, perhaps reflecting the absence of stabilising hydrophobic groove interactions (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a description of the crystal structure data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: AlphaFold3 correctly predicted the 4E-BP1/PDZ interaction regardless of phosphorylation status.
source: While the 4E-BP1/PDZ interaction was correctly predicted regardless of phosphorylation status (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 2E), only the phosphorylated substrate was predicted to interact directly with the PP1 active site.
evidence: This is based on AlphaFold3 modeling shown in the figures.

claim: AlphaFold3 predicted that only the phosphorylated 4E-BP1 substrate interacts directly with the PP1 active site.
source: While the 4E-BP1/PDZ interaction was correctly predicted regardless of phosphorylation status (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 2E), only the phosphorylated substrate was predicted to interact directly with the PP1 active site.
evidence: This is based on AlphaFold3 modeling shown in the figures.

claim: In the AlphaFold3 model, the 4E-BP1 substrate sequence 68TK(pT70)PPR73 docks at the PP1 catalytic site with high confidence.
source: The 4E-BP1 substrate sequence 68TK(pT70)PPR73, predicted with high confidence, docks at the catalytic site, with K69 interacting with D220PP1, pT70 interacting with the metal ions, H125PP1 and R221PP1, and P71 interacting with Y134PP1, but the remodelled PP1 hydrophobic groove remains unoccupied (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is based on AlphaFold3 modeling shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: In the AlphaFold3 model of phosphorylated 4E-BP1 with PP1-Neurabin, the remodelled PP1 hydrophobic groove remains unoccupied.
source: The 4E-BP1 substrate sequence 68TK(pT70)PPR73, predicted with high confidence, docks at the catalytic site, with K69 interacting with D220PP1, pT70 interacting with the metal ions, H125PP1 and R221PP1, and P71 interacting with Y134PP1, but the remodelled PP1 hydrophobic groove remains unoccupied (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is based on AlphaFold3 modeling shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: AlphaFold3 gives only a low confidence prediction for the unphosphorylated 4E-BP1 substrate interacting with PP1.
source: In contrast, AlphaFold3 gives only a low confidence prediction for the unphosphorylated substrate site D74 and L75 interacting with H125PP1 and Y134PP1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is based on AlphaFold3 modeling shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2D.

claim: AlphaFold3 predictions of full-length 5x phospho-4E-BP1 with Neurabin/PP1 placed the C-terminus of 4E-BP1 in the ligand-binding groove of the PDZ domain.
source: All the predictions placed the C-terminus of 4E-BP1 in the ligand-binding groove of the PDZ domain, docking the phosphorylated T70 site in the PP1 active site in a similar manner to that seen in the substrate chimera predictions (Figure 6F; Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is based on AlphaFold3 modeling shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The primary determinant of substrate specificity for Neurabin/PP1 is interaction with the PDZ domain adjacent to the RVxF-ΦΦ-R-W string.
source: Taken together with the crystallography and biochemical data, our observations support the view that the primary determinant of substrate specificity for Neurabin/PP1 is interaction with the PDZ domain adjacent to the RVxF-ΦΦ-R-W string.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined structural, biochemical, and modeling data.

claim: All four PP1-Phactr fusions exhibited virtually identical substrate specificities.
source: All four PP1-Phactr fusions exhibited virtually identical substrate specificities, which were substantially similar to that of the authentic Phactr1/PP1 holoenzyme, giving confidence that findings made with the fusions are also applicable to other RVxF-ΦΦ-R-W PIP/PP1 holoenzymes.
evidence: This is based on the phosphoproteomics data comparing the four PP1-Phactr fusions.

claim: Differential intracellular targeting and/or tissue-specific expression of the four different Phactr/PP1 holoenzymes likely allows further refinement of substrate specificity.
source: It is likely that differential intracellular targeting and/or tissue-specific expression of the four different Phactr/PP1 holoenzymes allows further refinement of substrate specificity.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that the four Phactrs have identical substrate specificities in vitro.

claim: For PNUTS, only the SET1A/B-COMPASS complex components CXXC1/CFP1 and SETD1B were identified as potential substrates.
source: For PNUTS, we identified only the SET1A/B-COMPASS complex components CXXC1/CFP1 and SETD1B (Cenik and Shilatifard, 2021).
evidence: This is based on the phosphoproteomics data for PP1-PNUTS.

claim: CXXC1/CFP1 and SETD1B may be recruited to PNUTS by interaction with its binding partner WDR82.
source: These may be recruited to PNUTS by interaction with its binding partner WDR82, which is also present in SET1A/B-COMPASS complexes (Cenik and Shilatifard, 2021), but further work will be necessary to confirm this.
evidence: This is speculation based on known protein interactions.

claim: The use of the PP1 fusion approach for PPP1R15A/B may be confounded by interaction of these PIPs with G-actin.
source: It is possible that the use of the PP1 fusion approach for these PIPs is confounded by interaction of these PIPs with G-actin (Chen et al., 2015; Yan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is speculation to explain why no substrates were identified for PP1-R15A/B fusions.

claim: Overexpression of PP1-Neurabin can suppress translation when expressed in 293 cells.
source: Consistent with this, we found that overexpression of PP1-Neurabin can suppress translation when expressed in 293 cells.
evidence: This is based on the protein synthesis assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Neurabin and Spinophilin can negatively regulate both arms of the mTORC1 protein synthesis pathway.
source: It is therefore likely that Neurabin and Spinophilin can negatively regulate both arms of the mTORC1 protein synthesis pathway (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is inferred from the identification of 4E-BPs and p70 S6K as substrates.

claim: The micromolar affinity of the 4E-BP1 PBM for the Neurabin/Spinophilin PDZ domains may reflect the necessity for effective competition with the mTORC1 kinase complex.
source: The micromolar affinity of this interaction, which is stronger than that previously reported for p70 S6K (Burnett et al., 1998), may reflect the necessity for effective competition with the mTORC1 kinase complex, which binds the 4E-BPs using a C-terminal TOS motif that overlaps the PBM (Schalm and Blenis, 2002; Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is speculation based on the measured binding affinities and known biology.

claim: Neurabin/Spinophilin oligomerisation and/or F-actin binding, and membrane localisation, may effectively increase the avidity of weak PBM-PDZ interactions.
source: It may be that Neurabin/Spinophilin oligomerisation and/or F-actin binding, and membrane localisation, effectively increases the avidity of such weak PBM-PDZ interactions, but more work is required to establish whether these channels are direct Neurabin/PP1 substrates.
evidence: This is speculation to explain how weak PDZ interactions might be functionally relevant.

claim: In the PP1-Neurabin fusion, the PIP sequences play a critical role in directing substrate specificity and potentiating catalytic efficiency.
source: In the context of the PP1-PIP fusions, and by extension in that of the PIP/PP1 holoenzyme, the PIP sequences play a critical role in directing substrate specificity and potentiating catalytic efficiency.
evidence: This is inferred from the peptide dephosphorylation assay data.

claim: The relatively low affinity of active site interaction in PP1-Neurabin allows dephosphorylation of multiple 4E-BP sites during one round of PDZ binding.
source: Our observations suggest a model in which 4E-BPs are recruited to Neurabin/PP1 via high-affinity PBM-PDZ interaction, with the relatively low affinity of active site interaction allowing dephosphorylation of the multiple sites during one round of PDZ binding (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the biochemical and structural data.

claim: The 'suboptimal' reactivity of 4E-BP1 with alanine substitutions at +1 and +2 may reflect a requirement to balance dephosphorylation rates between the multiple 4E-BP1 phosphorylation sites.
source: We speculate that this 'suboptimal' reactivity may reflect a requirement to balance dephosphorylation rates between the multiple 4E-BP1 phosphorylation sites, especially if multiple rounds of dephosphorylation occur for each PBM-PDZ interaction.
evidence: This is speculation to explain the unexpected increase in activity with certain mutations.

claim: A PIP could in principle recruit substrates through protein interactions and remodel the PP1 substrate binding grooves to allow discrimination between different phosphorylated sites on the target protein.
source: Although the remodelled hydrophobic groove does not play a role in 4E-BP recognition by Neurabin/PP1, this does not necessarily mean that sequence-specific dephosphorylation by other PIP/PP1 complexes and substrate recruitment by protein interactions are inherently mutually exclusive: in principle, a PIP could recruit substrates through protein interactions and remodel the PP1 substrate binding grooves to allow discrimination between different phosphorylated sites on the target protein.
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms for other PIP/PP1 complexes.

claim: The other RVxF-ΦΦ-R-W PIPs will likely also recruit substrates by interaction with other PIP domains or proteins bound to them.
source: That said, we think it likely that the other RVxF-ΦΦ-R-W PIPs will also recruit substrates by interaction with other PIP domains or proteins bound to them.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings with Neurabin/Spinophilin.

claim: Substrate recruitment interactions for other RVxF-ΦΦ-R-W PIPs might involve WDR82 for PNUTS and G-actin for PPP1R15A/B.
source: Such interactions might involve WDR82 for PNUTS and G-actin for PPP1R15A/B (Yan et al., 2021; Erickson et al., 2024).
evidence: This is speculation based on known protein interactions.

claim: Neurabin/PP1 and Spinophilin/PP1 holoenzymes are new candidate regulators of the mTORC1 pathway.
source: Our findings establish Neurabin/PP1 and Spinophilin/PP1 holoenzymes as new candidate regulators of the mTORC1 pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the identification of 4E-BPs and p70 S6K as substrates.

claim: Endogenous PP2Cγ/PPM1G contributes to 4E-BP1 dephosphorylation in 293 and HCT116 cells.
source: Many studies have focussed on mTORC1 regulation of translation on the control of cell growth, particularly in cancer settings (Liu and Sabatini, 2020), and previous work has shown that endogenous PP2Cγ/ PPM1G contributes to 4E-BP1 dephosphorylation in 293 and HCT116 cells (Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Localised translational regulation is important in neuronal development and function.
source: Localised translational regulation is also important in other settings, however, including neuronal development and function (Holt et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: mTORC1 signalling plays an important role in neuronal plasticity.
source: Here, mTORC1 signalling plays an important role in neuronal plasticity (Hoeffer and Klann, 2010), as do both Neurabin and Spinophilin, which are largely neuron-specific and enriched in dendritic spines (Wu et al., 2008, reviewed by Foley et al., 2021), and the 4E-BPs, particularly 4E-BP2 (for references, see Aguilar-Valles et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Neurabin and Spinophilin are largely neuron-specific and enriched in dendritic spines.
source: Here, mTORC1 signalling plays an important role in neuronal plasticity (Hoeffer and Klann, 2010), as do both Neurabin and Spinophilin, which are largely neuron-specific and enriched in dendritic spines (Wu et al., 2008, reviewed by Foley et al., 2021), and the 4E-BPs, particularly 4E-BP2 (for references, see Aguilar-Valles et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The finding that 4E-BPs are Neurabin/PP1 substrates potentially establishes a direct link between Neurabin and neuronal mTORC1 signalling.
source: Our finding that 4E-BPs are Neurabin/PP1 substrates potentially establishes a direct link between Neurabin and neuronal mTORC1 signalling (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), which will be an interesting topic for future investigation.
evidence: This is inferred from the identification of 4E-BPs as Neurabin/PP1 substrates.
